title: Non-decreasing Array
spaceBreakdown:
- int n, modified, i: three scalars → O(1)
- no containers, no recursion
- not counted: input vector (modified in place)
approach: Scan left to right and count positions where `nums[i] > nums[i+1]`. If a second violation is found, return false immediately. For the first violation, greedily repair in place: if `i == 0` or `nums[i-1] <= nums[i+1]`, lower `nums[i]` to `nums[i+1]` (safe because the left neighbor is satisfied); otherwise raise `nums[i+1]` to `nums[i]` (the only option that keeps the left side valid). This greedy choice is optimal because lowering is always preferred when it doesn't break the left neighbor-it keeps values small for future comparisons.
hints: When you encounter a single position where `nums[i] > nums[i+1]`, what information from the elements just outside this pair determines whether lowering `nums[i]` or raising `nums[i+1]` is the safe repair?
Linear scan with greedy in-place repair. In `[4,2,3]`, at `i=0` we see `4 > 2`; since `i == 0` (no left neighbor to violate), lower `nums[0]` to `2`, giving `[2,2,3]`.

**Boundary index (first element)** - the dip is at `i = 0`, so there is no left neighbor to check.
`Input: nums = [4,2,3]` → `Expected: true`
⚠️ Bug: always raising `nums[i+1]` instead of checking the left neighbor → produces `[4,4,3]`, sees `4 > 3`, returns `false`

**Must raise, not lower** - lowering `nums[i]` would break the left neighbor `nums[i-1]`.
`Input: nums = [5,7,1,8]` → `Expected: true`
⚠️ Bug: always setting `nums[i] = nums[i+1]` (lowering the left element) → produces `[5,1,1,8]`, sees `5 > 1`, returns `false`

**All elements equal** - no strict decrease exists anywhere.
`Input: nums = [1,1,1]` → `Expected: true`
⚠️ Bug: using `nums[i] >= nums[i+1]` as the violation test → counts two "violations", returns `false`

**Two dips, unfixable** - two separate decreases; one edit cannot fix both.
`Input: nums = [4,2,1]` → `Expected: false`
⚠️ Bug: not tracking that a modification was already made (no `modified` counter) → fixes first dip to `[2,2,1]`, then fixes second to `[2,1,1]`, returns `true`

followUps.q: What if you can modify at most `k` elements instead of at most one?
followUps.a: Replace the early `return false` on the second violation with a counter that allows up to `k` fixes. The same greedy choice (lower when the left neighbor allows, otherwise raise) remains optimal because each fix is local and lowering keeps values minimal for future comparisons. TC: O(n), SC: O(1).

followUps.q: What if the array arrives as a stream and you must decide online whether each new element keeps the array fixable?
followUps.a: Buffer the last two seen values in scalars and maintain the modification count. When a new element creates a dip, apply the same greedy decision using the buffered previous value as `nums[i-1]`. TC: O(n), SC: O(1).

followUps.q: What if you cannot modify the input array at all?
followUps.a: Track an `effectivePrev` scalar representing the value the previous element would have after any applied fix, plus the value before it for the neighbor check. When a dip is found, decide the fix by comparing the buffered left-neighbor value with `nums[i+1]`, then update `effectivePrev` to reflect the chosen repair. TC: O(n), SC: O(1).
